input: Phase equilibrium is a fascinating and truly foundational concept in the world of chemical engineering, and it plays a crucial role in understanding how mixtures behave. In this passage, we will delve into the intriguing case of a partially miscible liquid pair, exploring what happens when two liquids are mixed together but refuse to dissolve completely in one another. When such a pair is brought together, the liquids dissolve in each other only to a limited extent, and over a certain range of overall compositions the mixture does not form a single, uniform liquid. Instead, it separates into two distinct liquid phases, each of which is essentially a saturated solution: one phase is rich in the first liquid and contains as much of the second liquid as it can hold, while the other phase is rich in the second liquid and contains as much of the first as it can hold. Interestingly, within this range, the compositions of the two phases remain fixed at a given temperature and pressure, and changing the overall composition merely changes the relative amounts of the two phases rather than what each phase actually contains. Outside this range, the mixture exists as a single phase, because one liquid is perfectly capable of dissolving the whole of the other. The condition that governs this equilibrium is expressed in terms of chemical potential, which can be thought of as a measure of the tendency of a component to leave a phase. A component will move between the phases as long as its chemical potential differs between them, and this movement continues until the chemical potential of each component is exactly the same in both phases. Only later is this condition written down as an equation, but the underlying idea is simple: equilibrium is the state in which no component has any tendency to move. It is worth noting that equilibrium is not a static state at the molecular level, since molecules continue to cross the boundary between the phases in both directions; the crossings simply balance, so nothing changes overall, highlighting the dynamic nature of the balance that nature achieves.
target:
Two liquids that dissolve in each other only to a limited extent form a partially miscible pair. Mixed in suitable proportions at fixed temperature and pressure, such a pair does not give a single homogeneous liquid. The mixture separates instead into two liquid phases, each a saturated solution of one component in the other. One phase is rich in the first component and holds as much of the second as it can dissolve; the other phase is rich in the second component and holds as much of the first as it can dissolve. Between the two solubility limits, the composition of each phase is fixed by the temperature and pressure, and a change in the overall composition of the mixture changes only the amounts of the two phases, not what either phase contains. Outside those limits the mixture is a single phase, because one liquid can dissolve the whole of the other.

Equilibrium between the phases is stated in terms of chemical potential. The chemical potential of a component in a phase is its partial molar Gibbs energy in that phase, and it measures the tendency of the component to leave the phase. A component passes from one phase to the other while its chemical potential differs between the phases, and the transfer lowers the total Gibbs energy of the mixture. Transfer stops when the chemical potential of each component is the same in both phases. That equality, holding for every component, is the condition of phase equilibrium for the pair. The condition is commonly written as an equation that sets the chemical potential of each component in one phase equal to its chemical potential in the other phase, and the equality of fugacities used in applied work is the same condition in another form. At equilibrium the phases are not static: molecules of each component cross the interface in both directions at equal rates, so the compositions stay constant while exchange continues. A change of temperature displaces the compositions until the equalities hold again at the new state.
